title: Tell me about a time you disagreed with a decision but committed to it
prompt: Tell me about a time you strongly disagreed with a decision, voiced your concerns, but the group went the other way — and you committed to it anyway. What was the decision, how did you push back, and what did you do once it was made?
blurb: Disagree & commit: did they voice a real, reasoned dissent AND then genuinely back the decision — not sandbag it?

rubric.label: Situation & the decision
rubric.description: Clearly frames the decision at stake, the stakes involved, and where they stood versus the group.

rubric.label: Quality of the disagreement
rubric.description: Shows they raised a substantive, well-reasoned objection through the right channel — data or principle, not just a gut 'no' — and were heard.

rubric.label: How they committed
rubric.description: Describes concretely how THEY backed the decision once made — actively supported it, didn't undermine it or say 'I told you so', helped make it succeed.

rubric.label: Result & impact
rubric.description: States what happened — the decision's outcome, and how their commitment (not just compliance) affected it. Honest even if their side was right or wrong.

rubric.label: Reflection & maturity
rubric.description: Shows they can separate ego from outcome — value team velocity over being right, and update their view based on how it played out.

rubric.label: Communication & structure
rubric.description: Structured, concise, and candid about a genuinely uncomfortable situation.

reference.scenario: The candidate should recall a decision they genuinely opposed — an architecture choice, a product bet, a process change, a hiring or roadmap call — where they made their case, were overruled or the consensus went the other way, and then fully committed. The strongest answers show real dissent (not a token quibble) AND real commitment (not passive-aggressive compliance).
model_points: Situation: a specific, consequential decision and a genuine disagreement — not a trivial one — with the reasons they saw it differently.
Task: they took responsibility for voicing the concern clearly and through the right forum, with evidence or reasoning, before the decision was locked.
Action: once the decision was made, they explicitly chose to commit — communicated support to their team, executed as if it were their own idea, and did not relitigate or undermine it.
Action: where useful, they set up a way to measure whether the decision was working, so the group could course-correct on data rather than on who was right.
Result: the outcome — sometimes the decision worked and they were glad they committed; sometimes it didn't and the pre-agreed metrics let the team pivot fast. Either is fine if told honestly.

Reflection: values organizational speed and trust over personal vindication; knows disagree-and-commit means fully committing, and knows the rare cases where a concern is serious enough to escalate rather than commit.

probes.question: How strongly did you actually disagree? What was genuinely at stake — walk me through the substance of your objection.

probes.trigger: committed passively / just 'went along with it'
probes.question: What did committing actually look like in your day-to-day? Give me a concrete example of you actively supporting a decision you'd argued against.

probes.trigger: hints at 'I told you so' or undermining
probes.question: When it hit bumps, how did you talk about it with your team? Did you ever signal you'd been against it?
How did it turn out? Were you right, wrong, or somewhere in between — and how did you find out?
If you were right, how did the team learn that without it becoming about who won? And if you'd been wrong, would you have known?

red_flags: Never actually disagreed — story is really about agreeing all along, or the disagreement is trivial.
'Committed' but clearly sandbagged: slow-walked it, relitigated, or told the team it was doomed.
Says 'I told you so' or frames the whole story as being proven right.
Couldn't let it go — carried resentment, or escalated a normal decision past the point of reason.
No mechanism to learn whether the decision worked; commitment was blind compliance with no follow-through.
Blames the decision-maker for a bad outcome instead of owning their part in executing it.
follow_ups: Where's the line for you between disagree-and-commit and a concern serious enough that you must escalate or not commit?
How did you make sure the team behind you didn't lose motivation on a decision you'd opposed?
Have you ever failed to commit well? What happened?
How do you disagree in a way that gets you heard rather than dismissed?
reference.exemplar_answer: Situation: 'My team debated whether to rebuild our data pipeline in-house or adopt a managed service. I argued hard for building in-house — I thought the managed option would lock us in and cost more at scale — and I brought a cost model to back it.' Task: 'I made my case in the design review with numbers, but the tech lead and most of the team weighed faster time-to-market higher, and we went with the managed service.' Action: 'Once the call was made, I committed fully. I owned the integration, wrote the migration plan, and never framed it to the team as the wrong choice. I did propose we track cost-per-GB and lock-in risk quarterly so we'd have data if my concern ever materialized.' Result: 'We shipped roughly two months faster than an in-house build would have allowed, and the cost stayed reasonable at our volume — my concern was real but premature. The quarterly metric later flagged when costs did start climbing, and we revisited it calmly, on data.' Reflection: 'I learned that committing means genuinely rowing in the same direction, and that turning a disagreement into a measurable checkpoint beats being the person who was technically right. I'd still voice the dissent every time — but the value was in how I committed after.'

interviewer_notes: The two failure modes to distinguish: (1) never really disagreed — probe for substance and stakes; (2) never really committed — probe for concrete supportive actions and any hint of sandbagging or 'I told you so'. A strong answer has BOTH a real dissent and a real commitment. Watch for ego: candidates love stories where they were vindicated — push them to show the team learned it on data, not on who won. Senior maturity appears in knowing when disagree-and-commit does NOT apply (ethical or safety concerns warrant escalation, not commitment). Probe I-vs-we on the commitment actions specifically.
